title: Melbourne
wiki_lead:
Melbourne ( MEL-bərn, locally [ˈmæɫbən] ; Boonwurrung/Woiwurrung: Narrm or Naarm)  is the capital and most populous city of the Australian state of Victoria and the second-most populous city in Australia. The city's name generally refers to a 9,993-square-kilometre (3,858 sq mi) area, comprising an urban agglomeration of 30 local government areas. The name is also used specifically to refer to the local government area, also named the City of Melbourne, whose administrative area is centred on the Melbourne central business district and some immediate surrounds.
As of June 2025, the population of the city was 5.435 million, or 19% of the population of Australia. The city occupies much of the northern and eastern coastlines of Port Phillip Bay, it is claimed to be the southernmost city in the world with a population exceeding one million. Its inhabitants are known as "Melburnians".
The area of Melbourne has been home to Aboriginal Victorians for over 40,000 years. Of the five peoples of the Kulin nation, the traditional custodians of the land encompassing Melbourne are the Boonwurrung, Woiwurrung and the Wurundjeri peoples. In 1803, a short-lived British penal settlement was established at Port Phillip, then part of the Colony of New South Wales. Melbourne was founded in 1835 with the arrival of free settlers from Van Diemen's Land (modern-day Tasmania). It was incorporated as a Crown settlement in 1837 and named after the then Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne. Declared a city by Queen Victoria in 1847, it became the capital of the newly separated Colony of Victoria in 1851. During the 1850s Victorian gold rush, the city entered a lengthy boom period that, by the late 1880s, had transformed it into one of the largest and wealthiest metropolises in both Australia and the world. After the federation of Australia in 1901, Melbourne served as the interim seat of government of the new nation until Canberra became the permanent capital in 1927.
Today, Melbourne is a leading financial centre in the Asia-Pacific region, ranking 28th globally in the 2024 Global Financial Centres Index. The city's eclectic architecture blends Victorian-era structures, such as the World Heritage–listed Royal Exhibition Building, with a large skyline. Landmarks include the Melbourne Cricket Ground and the National Gallery of Victoria. Noted for its cultural heritage, the city gave rise to Australian rules football, Australian impressionism and Australian cinema, and is known for its street art, live music and theatre scenes. It hosts major annual sporting events, such as the Australian Grand Prix and the Australian Open Grand Slam, and also hosted the 1956 Summer Olympics. Melbourne ranked as the world's most liveable city on The Economist's measure for much of the 2010s. It was also voted the world's best city by Time Out in 2026.
Melbourne Airport is the second-busiest airport in Australia and the Port of Melbourne is the nation's busiest seaport. Its main metropolitan rail terminus is Flinders Street station and its main regional rail and road coach terminus is Southern Cross station. It also has Australia's most extensive freeway network and the largest urban tram network in the world.

Name
The Port Phillip area of Victoria was known in the Boonwurrung/Woiwurrung languages as Narrm or Naarm.
Different parts of Melbourne had different traditional Indigenous names, though these do not match up exactly with modern council districts. The Melbourne city area near St Paul's (or possibly St Patrick's) Cathedral was called Geeburr, the Fitzroy area was referred to as Ngár-go, and Collingwood was known as Yálla-birr-ang in the Woiwurrung language. The wider Port Phillip Bay area is referred to as Naarm in the Woiwurrung language; in the Boonwurrung language, Naarm means "the Bay".
The city is named after the British Prime Minister William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne, who was Prime Minister at the time of its founding
grok_lead: This article is about the Australian metropolitan area. For other uses, see Melbourne (disambiguation). Melbourne is the capital city of Victoria, the southeasternmost state of mainland Australia, and the nation's second-largest urban centre, with the Greater Melbourne metropolitan area encompassing over 5 million residents as of recent estimates. Situated on the lower reaches of the Yarra River where it meets the northern shore of Port Phillip, a large bay opening to Bass Strait, the city occupies undulating terrain in a temperate oceanic climate zone conducive to diverse urban development. Established in 1835 by free settlers arriving via the schooner Enterprize from Van Diemen's Land (modern Tasmania), the outpost was surveyed and named after William Lamb, 2nd Viscount Melbourne, the British prime minister at the time; it was proclaimed a town in 1837 and elevated to city status in 1847 under Queen Victoria. The city's economy, dominated by professional services, finance, education, health care, and manufacturing, generates an annual gross domestic product of approximately AU$369 billion for the metropolitan area, accounting for a substantial portion of Victoria's output and positioning Melbourne as Australia's premier capital for business activity. Its cultural landscape features world-renowned institutions like the National Gallery of Victoria and a thriving scene of street art, live music, and festivals, earning it recognition as Australia's cultural capital, while its sporting infrastructureâincluding the Melbourne Cricket Ground, host to international cricket and Australian rules footballâunderpins its status as the nation's sporting heart, with major events such as the Australian Open tennis grand slam and the Melbourne Cup horse race drawing global attention. Melbourne's growth accelerated dramatically during the Victorian gold rushes of the 1850s, transforming it into Australia's largest and wealthiest city by the 1860s, a position it held until Federation in 1901; it later served as the temporary national capital from 1901 to 1927 and hosted the 1956 Summer Olympics, cementing its role in international events.
